results.content: DNMTechs – Sharing and Storing Technology Knowledge Javascript, Python, Android, Bash, Hardware, Software and more… # Pinning Python Dependencies: Best Practices and Considerations When working with Python projects, managing dependencies is a crucial aspect of ensuring smooth and consistent development. However, pinning dependencies is an important practice to ensure that projects remain stable and reproducible over time. Pinning is the process of specifying exact versions of dependencies that a project requires. By pinning dependencies, developers ensure that the project will always use the same versions of libraries, regardless of any updates or changes made to those libraries in the future. By pinning all dependencies, developers have full control over the versions used in their project. However, updating dependencies should be done cautiously, ensuring compatibility and testing the project thoroughly after any updates. By regularly updating and reviewing dependencies, developers can ensure that their projects are protected against known vulnerabilities. With pinned dependencies, developers can easily recreate the same environment and ensure that the project behaves consistently across different systems. Continuous integration (CI) systems can automatically run tests against different versions of dependencies, ensuring that the project remains functional and compatible. In conclusion, pinning Python dependencies is a best practice that ensures stability, reproducibility, and compatibility in Python projects. By following the best practices and considerations mentioned above, developers can effectively manage their project’s dependencies and minimize potential issues. When it comes to managing dependencies in Python, pinning is an essential practice to ensure consistency and reproducibility across different environments. By pinning dependencies, you specify the exact versions of the packages your project relies on, preventing any unexpected or incompatible updates. ### Example 1: Pinning Dependencies in a requirements.txt file requests==2.25.1 pandas==1.2.3 numpy==1.20.1 In this example, we have a requirements.txt file that specifies the exact versions of the “requests,” “pandas,” and “numpy” packages. When pinning dependencies, it is important to regularly update them to benefit from bug fixes and security patches. By following these best practices and considerations, you can effectively manage your Python dependencies, ensuring stability and reproducibility in your projects. ### Reference Links: * Python Packaging User Guide - install\_requires vs requirements.txt ### Conclusion: Pinning Python dependencies is a crucial practice for maintaining consistency and reproducibility in software projects.

results.title: Reproducibility standards for machine learning in the life sciences - PMC
results.content: To make machine learning analyses in the life sciences more computationally reproducible, we propose standards based on data, model, and code publication, programming best practices, and workflow automation. 1. **The bronze standard:** the authors make the data, models, and code used in the analysis publicly available. Without data, models, and code, it is not possible to reproduce a work. 2. **The silver standard:** in addition to meeting the bronze standard, (1) the dependencies of the analysis can be downloaded and installed in a single command, (2) key details for reproducing the work are documented, including the order in which to run the analysis scripts, the operating system used, and system resource requirements, and (3) all random components in the analysis are set to be deterministic. 3. **The gold standard**: the work meets the silver standard, and the authors make the analysis reproducible with a single command. Without data, models can not be trained and analyses can not be reproduced. Even if the code for an analysis were perfectly reproducible and required no extra scientist-time to run, its corresponding model would still need to be made publicly available. Because of the importance of sharing trained models, meeting the bronze standard of reproducibility requires that authors deposit trained weights for the models used to generate their results in a public repository. While it is possible to reproduce an analysis with only its data, models, and code, this task is by no means easy. Accordingly, the silver standard requires that authors record the order in which one should run their analysis components, the operating system version used to produce the work, and the time taken to run the code. In short, by meeting the gold standard authors make the burden of reproducing their work as small as possible. Authors who strive to meet the bronze, silver, and gold standards will increase the reproducibility of machine learning analyses in the life sciences. We envision a reproducibility collaborator as someone outside the primary authors’ research groups who certifies that they were able to reproduce the results of the paper from only the data, models, code, and accompanying documentation.

results.title: Reproducible Forecasting Workflows | Ecological Forecasting Initiative
results.content: Version control is the process of managing changes in code and workflows and improves transparency in the code development process and facilitates open science and reproducibility. Software development is a trillion dollar industry and it is well worth the time learning the basics of industry standard tools like version control, rather than relying on ad hoc and error prone approaches such as file naming (e.g. script.v2.R, python\_script\_final\_FINAL.py), Dropbox/Google Drive, or emailing files to collaborators. These tools analyze workflows, skip phases of the workflow that are up-to-date (if the exact inputs and tasks have been run previously, the previous outputs can be returned; this technique is sometimes called memoization), and execute tasks that are out-of-date, tasks downstream of out-of-date tasks, or tasks required to execute based on scheduled run times (e.g., daily-updating forecast). These tools are especially useful for large projects that bring multiple streams of data together in an analysis since it relieves the analyst from duties of keeping track of workflow order and tasks that need to be rerun. Tools for continuous integration enable researchers to update their forecasts and run tests on their code in an automated and robust manner (e.g. with system tests in place to check for accidental deployments that would otherwise break a deployment). Continuous Integration (CI) tools automatically builds and deploys software ecosystems, and tests new versions of code to ensure development of models will work. Complex scientific workflows often involve combining multiple different tools written in different programming languages and/or possessing different software dependencies. Moreover, containerization software sometimes allows for the creation of **container stacks** (a.k.a **“orchestration”**)— collections of multiple containers that communicate with each other (including sharing data) and with the host system in precise, user-defined ways (see Workflow and Dependency Management above). A core principle of creating reproducible scientific workflows is making the code and data used in the analyses available to the public through data and code publication or releases. Additionally, embedding data publishing tasks (e.g. metadata descriptions, pushing data to a remote repository) in a dependency management system (see above) can make updating data in a public repository as easy as executing one line of code.
